name: Bigos
clues: It is said to improve every time it is reheated, so cooks deliberately make it days before it is eaten.
It is the food of the winter forest and the aristocratic hunt, and gets a passage of its own in Poland's national epic.
Soured shredded cabbage stewed for hours with several smoked meats, dried mushrooms and a handful of prunes.
Poland's long-simmered hunter's stew, built on sauerkraut and whatever game or sausage the household has.
fact: Adam Mickiewicz devoted lines of Pan Tadeusz to it, which helped cement its status as a national dish.

name: Żurek
clues: It depends on a jar of grain and water left to go sour on the windowsill for several days.
It is the Easter breakfast soup of Poland, sometimes served inside a hollowed loaf of bread.
A cloudy, tart, gently thickened broth heavy with marjoram, holding halved eggs and pale sausage.
The Polish sour rye soup with white sausage, egg and marjoram.
fact: The starter, zakwas, is fermented rye flour and water — the same principle as sourdough, but used as a liquid seasoning.

name: Pierogi
clues: The most classic filling is named after a Ukrainian city, though the dish is claimed firmly by its western neighbour.
They are boiled first and very often fried afterwards in butter, and a dozen fillings from savoury to sweet exist.
Half-moons of soft dough crimped by hand around a mash of potato and fresh curd, served with browned onion and cream.
The Polish filled dumpling, boiled then buttered, with the classic potato-and-curd filling named for Ruthenia.
fact: Ruskie pierogi are named for Red Ruthenia, not Russia — a distinction Poles are careful to make.

name: Lángos
clues: Its name comes from the word for flame, because it was once baked at the mouth of the bread oven while it was still roaring.
It is the food of the summer lakeside and the winter market stall, sold on a paper plate that immediately goes translucent.
A plate-sized round of yeasted dough deep-fried until blistered, rubbed with garlic and buried in cream and cheese.
The Hungarian deep-fried flatbread topped with soured cream and grated cheese.
fact: Adding mashed potato to the dough is the trick that keeps it soft inside rather than turning into a hard crust.

name: Chicken Paprikash
clues: The defining spice must never touch a hot pan directly or it turns irreversibly bitter — the pot comes off the heat first.
It is served with small torn egg dumplings that exist mainly to carry the sauce.
Poultry braised in an enormous quantity of onion and sweet ground pepper, finished with soured cream stirred in off the heat.
The Hungarian chicken stew in sweet paprika and soured cream, served with nokedli.
fact: Paprika arrived in Hungary via the Ottomans, and only became central to the national cuisine in the nineteenth century.

name: Sauerbraten
clues: Before any heat is applied it spends up to a week submerged, and that soak is the entire point.
The Rhineland version thickens its sauce with a crushed spiced Christmas biscuit, which sounds like a mistake and is not.
A joint made tender and distinctly sour by long marination, served in a dark sweet-sour gravy with raisins.
Germany's marinated pot roast, soured with vinegar and served with red cabbage and potato dumplings.
fact: The Rhenish version was historically made with horse meat, and some Cologne butchers still offer it that way.

name: Spätzle
clues: The name means little sparrows, and traditionally the batter is scraped off a wet board straight into boiling water.
A regional law of sorts insists the real thing has a rough, irregular surface, because that is what holds sauce.
Soft irregular egg-rich squiggles, boiled briefly then tossed in butter, sometimes layered with cheese and onions.
The Swabian soft egg noodle, served as a side or baked in a cheese-and-onion casserole.
fact: Swabian brides were once judged on whether their scraped noodles were thin enough to let light through.

name: Rösti
clues: The linguistic border of its home country is named after it, dividing those who eat it from those who do not.
It began as a farmer's breakfast in the canton of Bern, made from the previous day's boiled leftovers.
Coarsely grated tuber pressed into a pan and fried in butter until a deep golden crust forms on both faces.
The Swiss crisp grated potato cake, flipped whole and served in a wedge.
fact: The Röstigraben, or rösti ditch, is the informal name for the cultural divide between German- and French-speaking Switzerland.

name: Tartiflette
clues: It looks ancient but was essentially invented in the 1980s by a cheese marketing board to sell more of one specific wheel.
It belongs to the ski slopes of the French Alps, and one half of a washed-rind cheese is laid crust-up over the top.
Sliced potatoes baked with bacon, onion and white wine under a cheese that collapses into the dish as it melts.
The Savoyard baked potato and bacon gratin sealed with a whole halved reblochon.
fact: The Syndicat Interprofessionnel du Reblochon promoted the recipe in the 1980s, adapting an older dish called péla.

name: Cassoulet
clues: Three towns each claim their version is the true one, and locals speak of them as father, son and holy spirit.
It is named after the glazed earthenware vessel it is baked in, which slopes so the top can crust.
White beans baked for hours with preserved poultry and sausage until a skin forms, which is broken back in repeatedly.
The slow-baked bean and confit casserole of Castelnaudary, Carcassonne and Toulouse.
fact: Tradition says the crust should be broken and stirred back in seven times during baking.

name: Bouillabaisse
clues: Its name is a compressed instruction: bring it to the boil, then lower it.
It began as the Marseille fisherman's way of using the spiny rockfish nobody would buy at market.
The broth is strained off and served first with garlicky rust-coloured sauce on toast; the fish follows on a separate plate.
The Marseille fish soup, scented with saffron, fennel and orange peel, served with rouille and croutons.
fact: A 1980 charter signed by Marseille restaurateurs specifies which rockfish must be present for it to be sold under the name.

name: Pissaladière
clues: It is named after a fermented fish paste that most modern versions no longer contain.
It is sold by the slab in the markets of the old town of a Riviera city that was Italian until 1860.
A bread base under a deep layer of onions cooked to jam, latticed with salted fillets and studded with olives.
The Niçoise onion tart with anchovies and black olives, eaten at room temperature.
fact: Pissalat, the original anchovy condiment, gave the dish its name and is now made by only a handful of producers.

name: Fabada Asturiana
clues: The beans have their own protected designation, and they must never be stirred with a spoon — the pot is shaken instead.
It comes from a green, rainy, cider-drinking region on Spain's northern coast that feels nothing like the Mediterranean.
Large buttery white beans stewed with smoked blood sausage and paprika sausage until the broth goes orange and unctuous.
The Asturian bean stew with chorizo, morcilla and cured pork shoulder.
fact: The compango — the trio of cured meats — is sold as a matched set specifically for this dish.

name: Pulpo a la Gallega
clues: The cook dips it into boiling water three times before letting it cook, a ritual said to stop the skin from tearing.
It is festival food in Spain's rainy north-west, served on round wooden plates by specialist cooks called pulpeiras.
Thick tender rounds cut with scissors, laid over potato and dusted with smoked pepper, with a slick of good oil.
The Galician dish of boiled octopus with paprika and olive oil, served on a wooden plate.
fact: Copper pots are traditional, and a wine cork is often dropped in — folklore says it helps tenderise the octopus.

name: Gazpacho
clues: It predates the arrival of its now-defining red ingredient from the Americas by centuries — the original was white.
It is drunk as much as eaten, sometimes from a glass, during the ferocious southern Spanish summer.
Raw vegetables and soaked bread blended cold and emulsified with oil until smooth and faintly pink-orange.
The chilled raw Andalusian tomato and bread soup, sharpened with sherry vinegar.
fact: Ajo blanco, the older almond-and-garlic version, survives as its own dish in Málaga.

name: Bacalhau à Brás
clues: Its main ingredient is preserved in a way that requires two days of soaking with several water changes before it can be used.
It is named after a tavern keeper from the Bairro Alto district of Lisbon.
Shredded fish, straw-thin fried potato and egg stirred together over low heat so the egg binds but never sets into an omelette.
The Lisbon dish of shredded salt cod with matchstick potatoes bound in soft scrambled egg.
fact: Portugal claims a different salt cod recipe for every day of the year, and this is among the most ordered.

name: Francesinha
clues: Its name means little French girl, and it is an emigrant's attempt to reproduce a croque-monsieur with local ambition.
It belongs to Porto, and is usually surrounded by a moat of chips to soak up what runs off it.
A stacked sandwich of three or four meats, sealed under melted cheese and flooded with a hot beer-and-tomato sauce.
Porto's cheese-covered meat sandwich drowned in spiced beer sauce, served with chips.
fact: Daniel da Silva, a returning emigrant from France and Belgium, is credited with creating it in the 1950s.

name: Cacio e Pepe
clues: It has only three components, and precisely that is what makes it one of the hardest things in its cuisine to get right.
It was shepherds' food: everything in it keeps for weeks in a saddlebag without refrigeration.
A sauce made from nothing but grated sheep's cheese, cracked pepper and starchy cooking water emulsified into a cream.
The Roman pasta of pecorino and black pepper, with no cream, butter or garlic whatsoever.
fact: Overheating the cheese makes it seize into strings, which is why the pan must come off the heat before it goes in.

name: Vitello Tonnato
clues: It pairs a land animal with a sea one in a way that sounds wrong on paper and is a classic in practice.
It is the standard opener of a Piedmontese Christmas lunch, served cold and sliced paper-thin.
Pale poached meat under a pourable pale sauce built on preserved fish, capers and egg yolk.
The Piedmontese cold dish of thinly sliced veal under a tuna and caper sauce.
fact: The oldest versions had no tuna at all — the name likely came from a term for the way the meat was preserved in oil.

name: Risotto alla Milanese
clues: Legend blames a glassmaker's apprentice who used a pigment from his master's workshop as a prank at a wedding feast.
It is the traditional partner to a bone-in braised veal shin from the same city.
Short grains cooked slowly with stock until creamy but still firm at the core, turned gold by a single costly spice.
Lombardy's saffron rice dish, finished with butter and parmesan and traditionally enriched with marrow.
fact: The final vigorous beating in of cold butter and cheese off the heat is called the mantecatura, and it makes the texture.

name: Ribollita
clues: Its name refers to what happens on the second day, which is when it is considered ready.
It depends on a famously saltless local loaf, and on a dark crinkled winter cabbage that needs frost to sweeten.
So thick with soaked bread and pulses that a spoon stands up in it, finished with raw green oil poured over.
The Tuscan peasant soup of black cabbage, beans and stale bread, reheated and thickened the next day.
fact: Tuscan bread is made without salt, which is why it goes stale rather than mouldy and works so well soaked in soup.

name: Arancini
clues: Its name means little oranges, for the colour and shape it takes once fried.
One half of its island argues for a feminine name and a round shape, the other for a masculine name and a cone.
A breaded and fried sphere of saffron rice hiding a pocket of meat sauce, peas and melting cheese.
The Sicilian deep-fried stuffed rice ball, filled with ragù and mozzarella.
fact: The conical eastern Sicilian shape is said to imitate Mount Etna, complete with a lava-like meat filling.

name: Avgolemono
clues: The technique at its heart is a nervous one: hot liquid must be dribbled into the eggs, never the reverse.
It is the standard convalescent food of Greek households and the traditional Easter soup in a lamb-based version.
A pale, velvety, sharply citrus broth thickened without any flour or cream at all.
The Greek chicken soup thickened with an emulsion of beaten egg and lemon juice.
fact: It is likely descended from the Sephardic agristada, a sauce of egg and sour juice carried into Greece from Spain.

name: Spanakopita
clues: The greens must be salted and wrung out hard, or the whole structure collapses into a soggy failure.
It belongs to a huge family of Greek pies, and in Epirus wild foraged greens replace the cultivated leaf.
Layer upon layer of brushed tissue pastry enclosing greens bound with a salty white brined cheese and dill.
The Greek filo pie filled with spinach and feta.
fact: Its wild-greens cousin, hortopita, uses a foraged mix that can include nettle, dandelion and fennel fronds.

name: Smørrebrød
clues: There is an etiquette to the order in which you eat them, and using a top slice of bread is considered wrong.
It is lunch in Denmark, taken with cold beer and a shot of caraway spirit.
A dense dark sour loaf, buttered to the very edges, carrying a carefully composed single layer of toppings.
The Danish open-faced rye sandwich, most classically topped with pickled herring or prawns.
fact: The butter layer is functional, not decorative: it waterproofs the rye against the wet toppings.

name: Gravlax
clues: Its name literally means buried, because medieval fishermen packed it in sand above the tideline to ferment.
It is served at the Nordic Christmas table with a sweet mustard and dill sauce.
Never cooked and never smoked, just weighted under salt, sugar and herbs for a couple of days until firm and translucent.
The Scandinavian salmon cured with salt, sugar and dill, sliced thin and served with mustard sauce.
fact: The medieval original really was lightly fermented; the modern version is a straightforward cure with no fermentation at all.

name: Surströmming
clues: Several airlines have banned it from cabins on the grounds that the containers can burst.
It is traditionally opened outdoors, under water, on the third Thursday of August.
Small fish left in weak brine to ferment for months until the tin bulges and the smell precedes it by some distance.
The Swedish fermented Baltic herring, eaten in a flatbread roll with potato, onion and sour cream.
fact: The tin continues to ferment on the shelf, which is why it swells — and why it is opened submerged in water.

name: Haggis
clues: A poem is recited to it and a knife plunged into it before anyone is allowed to eat, every January.
Despite its national associations, the earliest written recipes for something like it are English.
Minced offal bound with toasted oats and suet, heavily peppered, cooked inside a natural casing until it can be cut open.
Scotland's pudding of sheep's offal and oatmeal, served with mashed neeps and tatties.
fact: Robert Burns' 1786 Address to a Haggis is what turned a common peasant dish into a national symbol.

name: Cullen Skink
clues: The second half of its name is an old Scots word for shin or broth, not a comment on its smell.
It is named after a fishing town on the Moray Firth, which hosts an annual championship for making it.
A thick pale soup of milk and floury potato carrying flakes of pale gold smoked fish.
The Scottish soup of smoked haddock, potato and onion in milk.
fact: Proper versions use Finnan haddie — cold-smoked undyed haddock — rather than the bright yellow dyed fillets.

name: Toad in the Hole
clues: Its name imagines small creatures peeking out of a burrow, which is roughly what the finished dish looks like.
It began as a way of stretching a little meat with a lot of cheap batter, and eighteenth-century versions used any leftover joint.
A batter of flour, egg and milk poured over meat into a smoking-hot fatted tin, where it climbs the sides as it bakes.
The English dish of sausages baked into Yorkshire pudding batter, served with onion gravy.
fact: The tin and fat must be genuinely smoking before the batter goes in, or the pudding will not rise around the sausages.

name: Borscht
clues: UNESCO placed it on a list of endangered cultural heritage in 2022, which was itself a political act.
It is served with small garlic rolls, and the deepest colour is preserved by adding acid near the end of cooking.
A crimson soup of root vegetables and cabbage, sharp as well as sweet, finished with a white swirl and dill.
The Ukrainian beetroot soup served with soured cream and garlic bread rolls.
fact: The earliest versions were made from fermented hogweed, and beetroot only became standard much later.

name: Adjaruli Khachapuri
clues: Its shape is meant to evoke a boat on the Black Sea, with the yolk standing in for the setting sun.
Its home region on the coast gives it its name, and the country has an index that tracks its cost as a measure of inflation.
An open bread vessel filled with molten brined cheese, finished with a raw yolk and butter stirred in at the table.
The boat-shaped Georgian cheese bread from Adjara, topped with an egg yolk and butter.
fact: You eat it by tearing off the pointed ends and using them to stir the yolk and butter into the cheese.

name: Khinkali
clues: The twisted knot on top is a handle, not part of the meal, and leaving a pile of them is how you count what you ate.
It comes from the mountain regions of a Caucasus country, and pepper is the only correct condiment.
A thick pleated pouch holding spiced raw mince that releases a mouthful of broth when you bite the side.
The Georgian soup dumpling, held by its topknot and eaten from the hand.
fact: Eating the doughy topknot is considered bad form; the discarded stems are counted at the end of the meal.

name: Ćevapi
clues: They descend from the Ottoman kebab tradition and are always ordered in odd numbers, five or ten at a time.
The bread they come in is held over the grill first so it soaks up the fat dripping from them.
Small skinless fingers of minced meat grilled over charcoal, packed into a puffy flatbread with raw onion.
The Balkan grilled minced-meat fingers served in somun with onion and clotted cream.
fact: Sarajevo's version is beef-only and traditionally served in tens, while Banja Luka's are grilled in joined groups of four.

name: Chicken Parmigiana
clues: A breaded, pan-fried cutlet gets baked beneath a blanket of tomato sauce and melted cheese until bubbling — a dish born more in immigrant kitchens abroad than in Italy itself.
The cutlet is pounded thin, dredged in egg and crumbs, fried until golden, then finished under the broiler so the cheese melts into a bubbling crust.
Its name nods to a hard, nutty grating cheese from a specific Italian region — ironic, since the cheese actually melted on top is usually a stretchier, milder one instead.
The Italian-American classic of a breaded, fried chicken cutlet baked under tomato sauce and melted cheese, named for a cheese from the city of Parma.
fact: Despite its Italian name honoring Parmigiano cheese, the dish as we know it — breaded chicken drowned in tomato sauce and mozzarella — was invented by Italian immigrants in the United States, not in Italy.

name: Chicken Marsala
clues: A thin cutlet simmers in a glossy sauce built from a fortified wine and mushrooms, with no tomato in sight.
The cutlet is lightly dusted in flour rather than crusted in crumbs, then pan-seared before the sauce reduces around it.
The sauce's signature comes from a Sicilian fortified wine named after its port city, mixed with sautéed mushrooms and a knob of butter.
The Italian-American dish of a flour-dusted chicken cutlet napped in a mushroom sauce built on a fortified Sicilian wine.
fact: Marsala wine, the fortified base of this dish's sauce, was originally developed in the 18th century by a British merchant trying to compete with Spanish sherry and Portuguese port.

name: Chicken Piccata
clues: A thin, quickly pan-fried cutlet is finished in a bright, tangy pan sauce built on citrus and small pickled buds, with no cheese or tomato involved.
The cutlet is pounded thin and dredged lightly in flour, then a fast sauce is built right in the same pan from butter, wine, and a sharp yellow citrus.
Its name comes from an Italian word describing a piquant, sharp style of preparation — sour and salty in careful balance.
The lemon-and-caper pan sauce classic, made with a quickly seared, flour-dusted chicken cutlet and a splash of white wine.
fact: The word 'piccata' describes a cooking style — sliced, sautéed, and served in a piquant sauce — that was originally applied to veal long before chicken became the more common, budget-friendly substitute.

name: Chicken Cacciatore
clues: Bone-in pieces of poultry braise low and slow in a rustic stew of tomatoes, peppers, onions, and herbs — no breading, no delicate cutlet here.
Its Italian name describes a rustic, forager's approach to supper, cooked the way someone returning from a day in the woods might improvise a meal from whatever was on hand.
Mushrooms, red wine, and bay leaf often join the pot, simmering until the meat falls easily from the bone.
The rustic Italian braise known in English by a name meaning 'hunter-style,' simmered with tomatoes, peppers, and onions.
fact: Cacciatore dishes have no single fixed recipe in Italy — some regions add tomatoes, others skip them entirely in favor of a white-wine-and-herb version, since the name only describes the rustic cooking style, not specific ingredients.

name: Ossobuco alla Milanese
clues: A cross-cut section of leg, bone and marrow still in the center, braises for hours in wine and broth until the meat surrenders to a fork.
It's traditionally eaten with a special narrow implement used just to scoop out the prized marrow at the bone's center.
It's finished with a raw garnish of lemon zest, garlic, and parsley chopped fine, scattered on top just before serving.
This braised veal shank, marrow still in the bone, is a specialty of Northern Italy's fashion capital, traditionally served with saffron risotto and a lemon-garlic-parsley garnish.
fact: The dish's name literally means 'bone with a hole,' referring to the marrow-filled cavity at the center of the cross-cut shank, which is traditionally eaten with a small specialized spoon.

name: Cotoletta alla Milanese
clues: A rib chop, bone left attached, is coated in golden crumbs and fried in butter until the crust shatters at the first bite.
Historians have long argued whether this crumbed, fried chop or a famous Austrian schnitzel came first, given centuries of trade between the two cities.
The bone is traditionally left in as a handle, and the meat is pounded thin while the rib stays intact, unlike a boneless escalope.
A bone-in, butter-fried breaded veal chop from the city famous for fashion and risotto, often set beside a wedge of lemon.
fact: A centuries-old rivalry claims this breaded veal chop predates Vienna's famous schnitzel, with some historians pointing to 12th-century Milanese monastery records as evidence, though the debate remains unresolved.

name: Saltimbocca alla Romana
clues: A thin escalope is topped with a slice of cured ham and a single fresh herb leaf, pinned in place before a quick sear in butter.
Its name translates loosely to 'jumps in the mouth,' a nod to how fast and vivid the flavor hits once it's plated.
No breadcrumb crust here — the herb and cured meat are seared directly onto the surface, then a splash of wine deglazes the pan into a light sauce.
A veal escalope from central Italy, topped with prosciutto and a sage leaf, pan-seared and finished with a wine sauce, whose name literally means 'jumps in the mouth.'
fact: Legend holds the dish got its name from diners at a Roman restaurant reacting so quickly and enthusiastically to its flavor that a poet exclaimed it truly 'jumped in the mouth.'

name: Bistecca alla Fiorentina
clues: A thick, hefty cut of beef from a prized white cattle breed is grilled hard and fast over hardwood embers, served intensely rare no matter what you ask for.
Seasoning stays deliberately minimal — coarse salt, cracked pepper, and a drizzle of good olive oil added only after it leaves the fire.
The cut includes both the tenderloin and the strip of loin on either side of a distinctive T-shaped divider, and it's traditionally priced and sold by weight per person.
The Tuscan grilled T-bone, cut thick from prized white cattle and served bone-in, rare, with nothing more than salt and olive oil.
fact: Traditionalists insist the steak must come from the Chianina, one of the oldest and largest cattle breeds in the world, and that asking for it well-done is close to a culinary crime in Florence.

name: Polpette
clues: Small hand-rolled balls of ground meat, bound with stale bread soaked in milk and a beaten egg, get browned before finishing in a simmering red sauce.
In their homeland they're rarely piled onto a plate of long strands the way abroad they famously are — that pairing is largely a foreign invention.
Grated hard cheese and a fistful of chopped parsley usually go into the mixture itself, not just sprinkled on top at the end.
Italy's version of hand-rolled meatballs, simmered in tomato sauce and rarely served atop spaghetti the way immigrants popularized abroad.
fact: In Italy, meatballs are traditionally served on their own as a second course, often smaller than a golf ball — the giant meatball perched on a mountain of spaghetti is largely an Italian-American creation.

name: Porchetta
clues: An entire deboned animal is butterflied, seasoned deep inside with garlic and wild herbs, then rolled tight and slow-roasted until the skin turns to shattering crackling.
Its aroma often comes from a golden pollen harvested from a feathery herb plant, rubbed generously into the meat before rolling.
Street vendors at countryside festivals slice it thin and stuff it straight into a crusty bread roll, crackling included in every bite.
Central Italy's whole roasted, herb-stuffed pork roll, famous for its crackling skin and sold sliced into sandwiches at festivals.
fact: Porchetta traces back over two thousand years to pre-Roman central Italy, where whole roasted, herb-stuffed pig was already a festival centerpiece long before it became a beloved street food.

name: Veal Scaloppine
clues: Thin slices of meat are pounded even thinner, dusted lightly in flour, and seared for barely a minute per side in a hot pan.
This is the base technique behind several fancier-named dishes — strip away the capers, the cured ham, or the mushrooms, and what's left is this simple preparation.
A quick pan sauce, often just butter, a splash of wine, and pan drippings, gets spooned over the top just before serving.
The foundational Italian technique of a thin, quickly pan-fried cutlet of meat finished in a light butter-and-wine sauce, the base for many dressed-up cousins.
fact: The word 'scaloppine' simply means 'small escalopes' in Italian and describes a technique, not a fixed recipe — nearly every sauced veal dish on this list is technically a variation of it.

name: Pollo Arrosto
clues: A whole bird is stuffed with citrus and herbs, trussed, and roasted until the skin crisps deep golden and the meat pulls easily from the bone.
Potatoes often roast alongside in the same pan, soaking up the rendered fat and pan juices as the bird cooks.
Unlike its breaded or sauced cousins, this version relies on nothing more than olive oil, garlic, lemon, and a sprig of herb tucked inside the cavity.
Italy's classic whole roasted chicken, stuffed with lemon and rosemary and often roasted beside potatoes in its own juices.
fact: In much of Italy, a whole roast chicken is traditionally a Sunday lunch centerpiece, often picked up already cooked from a rosticceria rather than made at home.

name: Minestrone
clues: This Italian vegetable stew has no single fixed recipe — cooks build it from whatever beans, greens and roots are in season, always simmered low and slow.
A rind of hard aged cheese is often dropped into the pot while it cooks, then fished out before serving to add a savory depth.
It's thick enough to stand a spoon in, commonly finished with a drizzle of olive oil and sometimes short pasta or rice stirred in near the end.
The classic Italian mixed-vegetable-and-bean soup, cooked slow and often finished with a parmesan rind.
fact: The name comes from the Italian verb 'minestrare,' meaning 'to serve' — it began as a catch-all peasant dish rather than a fixed recipe.

name: Pasta e Fagioli
clues: Small pasta shapes are simmered directly in a thick bean broth until they're barely tender, thickening the whole pot as their starch is released.
Italian immigrants carried a version of this dish to America, where it picked up an anglicized nickname among diners at old-school red-sauce restaurants.
A soffritto of garlic, rosemary and olive oil forms its backbone, and it's often finished with a hard grated cheese and a crack of black pepper.
Literally 'pasta and beans' in Italian, this rustic peasant classic simmers noodles right in the bean broth.
fact: In Italian-American communities the dish earned the nickname 'pasta fazool,' popularized in songs and mob movies from a dialect pronunciation of its second word.

name: Pappa al Pomodoro
clues: Born from Tuscan thrift, this dish exists to rescue stale, day-old loaves rather than waste them.
Chunks of dry bread are torn into a garlicky simmer of ripe summer produce until they dissolve into a thick, rustic mash.
It's traditionally served lukewarm rather than piping hot, generously drizzled with fruity olive oil and torn basil leaves.
A humble Tuscan bread-and-tomato mash, traditionally drizzled with olive oil and eaten just warm.
fact: The dish is immortalized in a beloved 1965 Italian pop song, 'Viva la pappa col pomodoro,' sung by child star Rita Pavone.

name: Stracciatella
clues: A beaten mixture of eggs, hard cheese and a pinch of nutmeg is whisked into simmering broth, where it sets into fine, ragged shreds within seconds.
Its name in Italian describes something 'torn into little rags,' referring to the delicate strands the egg forms as it cooks.
This quick classic from central Italy is a cousin to a well-known East Asian soup that uses the identical whisked-egg-into-broth technique.
Rome's whisked-egg broth soup, its name meaning 'little rags' for the shredded egg ribbons it forms — the Italian cousin of egg drop soup.
fact: This soup shares its name — and its 'shredded rag' technique — with the famous stracciatella gelato and cheese, all named for the same fine, torn strands.

name: Zuppa Toscana
clues: Crumbled spicy cured pork is browned first, then simmered with cubed potatoes, dark leafy greens and a splash of cream for richness.
This central Italian soup shares its home region with hearty bread soups and bean stews, and leans on rustic, cold-weather farmhouse ingredients.
It became a runaway hit at a popular American chain restaurant, where bottomless bowls of it are served alongside breadsticks and salad.
The creamy Italian sausage, potato and kale soup made famous stateside by Olive Garden.
fact: Though its name simply means 'Tuscan soup,' this creamy sausage-and-kale version was largely popularized by the American chain Olive Garden and is barely recognized by that name in Tuscany itself.

name: Tortellini in Brodo
clues: Tiny ring-shaped pasta parcels are stuffed with a rich mix of three meats and cheese, then pinched closed by hand around a fingertip.
Legend says a Bolognese innkeeper spied Venus's navel through a keyhole and shaped this pasta to imitate it.
It's a treasured Christmas Eve tradition in Emilia-Romagna, where the little stuffed pasta rings are served floating in a clear, slow-simmered capon or beef stock.
Emilia-Romagna's stuffed pasta rings, traditionally served floating in a clear meat broth at Christmas.
fact: According to Bolognese legend, this pasta's navel-like shape was inspired by an innkeeper glimpsing the goddess Venus's belly button through a keyhole.
